scenes.label: Meet the team
scenes.title: An official-looking warning
scenes.caption: Kabir sees a fictional bank-account warning with a familiar display name and a support number. Another message claims a courier problem. Both ask him to act through the links they supply.

scenes.label: The problem
scenes.title: Look behind the display name
scenes.caption: The message’s actual address does not match the supplied official-source pack. The claimed support number appears only inside the warning. A logo, polished grammar or a top search result does not independently establish authority.
scenes.dialogue: Display name and actual sender are different fields.

scenes.label: How it works
scenes.title: Choose a separate route
scenes.caption: Open a previously installed trusted app or use a contact obtained independently from the organisation’s genuine channel. Do not let the suspicious message choose the site, number and evidence used to verify itself.

scenes.label: Your decision
scenes.title: Test the claim
scenes.caption: The warning offers an urgent support call from its own number. Should Kabir call that number, trust the logo, or check using his existing trusted bank app?
scenes.dialogue: A support label does not authorise the caller.

scenes.label: What changes
scenes.title: A claim-to-evidence table
scenes.caption: Kabir records the account-lock claim and the independent check needed to resolve it. He keeps uncertainty visible instead of declaring the account safe from the message alone.
scenes.dialogue: Record what is claimed and what could verify it.

scenes.label: Enter the lab
scenes.title: Enter the verification lab
scenes.caption: Inspect sender details, match claims to independent checks and handle a well-written warning with no obvious spelling errors. The same evidence standard applies even when the message looks professional.
scenes.dialogue: Appearance is one observation, not the verdict.
